headline: Quick Pulse: Speaking Follow-Ups for ESL Warm-Ups
problemStatement: A poll can show what a class thinks without helping students explain why. Quick Pulse turns a fast phone response into a speaking prompt: students answer a question, review a visual class result, and hear classmates explain different views. Teachers can use it to warm up a topic or check understanding.
outcomes: Practice making a quick choice and then explaining the reason behind it aloud.
Compare class opinions through animated results that make a split easy to see.
Give students practice responding to a teacher question or one they create themselves.
howItWorks: Start with a short set of prompts. Students answer each prompt on their phones using a Yes/No choice or a 1-to-5 scale.
The class result appears as animated columns for a rating question or a tug-of-war view for a Yes/No question.
Use Ask both sides to hear from voters at opposite ends of the result, then ask why. The teacher can invite more students when the class needs a second voice.
Ask your own adds a yes/no or rating prompt, so the teacher can bring a fresh question into the pulse instead of being limited to a fixed set.
teacherUseCases: Open a lesson with a low-stakes question that gives every student a response before anyone speaks to the whole group.
Pause after a result and ask two classmates to explain different answers, turning the chart into a short discussion.

faq.a: A pulse can use a Yes/No response or a five-point agreement scale. Students answer on their phones, and the teacher sees a class-level result.

faq.q: Does Quick Pulse always use three prompts?
faq.a: It begins with a short set of mini-prompts, and the teacher can add an original question with Ask your own. The activity can therefore continue beyond the starter set.

faq.q: How do I get students talking after the vote?
faq.a: Ask both sides selects students from different ends of the result and invites them to say why. The teacher can repeat the follow-up with other voters.

faq.q: Can a quick poll work as a lesson check?
faq.a: Yes. Ask a question tied to the topic, inspect the class pattern, and invite students to explain answers. The result is a discussion cue rather than an automatic grade.
